title: Machine Learning Fundamentals
blurb: Classical ML — not because you'll train SVMs in production, but because every concept in deep learning has its roots here. Bias-variance, regularization, and evaluation are the load-bearing ideas.

nodes.label: The supervised learning loop
nodes.description: Inputs, labels, a loss function, an optimizer, iteration. The same six-step mental model that every model in this roadmap reduces to.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe the supervised loop and locate every component in any ML codebase you read.

resources.title: Stanford CS229 — Machine Learning
resources.author: Andrew Ng
resources.annotation: The canonical intro ML course. Lecture notes are clean and freely downloadable; the videos cover the supervised loop's whole vocabulary.

resources.title: Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow (3e)
resources.author: Aurélien Géron
resources.annotation: The practitioner's intro. The first half (classical ML with scikit-learn) is the cleanest 'supervised loop in code' you can read.

nodes.label: Linear regression
nodes.description: The simplest model that still teaches everything: parameters, loss, the normal equation vs gradient descent, regularization (ridge, lasso). Build it from scratch once.
nodes.doneWhen: You can implement linear regression from scratch in NumPy, with and without regularization.

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning (with Python)
resources.author: James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani
resources.annotation: Free PDF. The chapter on linear regression is the single best primer; pair with the labs to lock it in.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Linear Models
resources.annotation: The reference for the working flavor: ordinary least squares, ridge, lasso, elastic net. Read the docs alongside ISL.

nodes.label: Logistic regression
nodes.description: Binary classification, the sigmoid, the log-loss, decision boundaries. The conceptual root of every classifier head you'll write later.
nodes.doneWhen: You can derive the log-loss gradient and explain why logistic regression is a one-layer neural net.

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning — Chapter on Classification
resources.author: James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani
resources.annotation: Free PDF. The classification chapter walks logistic regression with the same clarity as the linear chapter.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Logistic Regression
resources.annotation: Multinomial, regularization, solvers — the practical knobs. Read after you understand the math.

nodes.label: Decision trees & random forests
nodes.description: How a tree splits, information gain, ensembles, why a random forest works. Still the right tool for many tabular problems in 2026.
nodes.doneWhen: You can explain why a single tree overfits and why bagging reduces variance.

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning — Trees
resources.author: James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani
resources.annotation: The trees chapter explains splits, bagging, random forests, and boosting with the same gentle clarity.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Decision Trees
resources.annotation: The practical interface plus the math. Pair with the ensemble docs for forests.

nodes.label: Gradient boosting (XGBoost / LightGBM)
nodes.description: Boosting as additive modeling, gradient boosting, XGBoost and LightGBM. The default winner on tabular benchmarks; you'll meet it in interviews and in production.
nodes.doneWhen: You can train a gradient-boosted model on a tabular dataset and explain its hyperparameters.

resources.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
resources.author: Chen & Guestrin
resources.annotation: The original XGBoost paper. The math is approachable and grounds the hyperparameter intuition.

resources.title: XGBoost — official documentation
resources.annotation: The actual reference you'll keep open while you tune. The parameter tuning page is gold.

nodes.label: k-means & clustering
nodes.description: Unsupervised learning's hello-world. k-means, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, when each one wins. Useful intuition for embedding spaces later.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick a clustering algorithm for a dataset and justify the choice.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Clustering
resources.annotation: The single most-useful page: the comparison table of clustering algorithms with their strengths and failure modes.

resources.title: k-means visualized
resources.author: Naftali Harris
resources.annotation: Click-through animation of the algorithm. Five minutes; the intuition sticks.

nodes.label: Dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP)
nodes.description: Compressing high-dimensional data while preserving structure. PCA (linear), t-SNE (local), UMAP (global+local). Critical for understanding embedding spaces.
nodes.doneWhen: You can choose between PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP for a visualization task and defend the choice.

resources.title: How to Use t-SNE Effectively
resources.author: Wattenberg, Viégas, Johnson
resources.annotation: Interactive Distill article. The 'how to not get fooled by your own t-SNE plot' resource.

resources.title: Understanding UMAP
resources.author: Coenen & Pearce
resources.annotation: The same idea as the t-SNE Distill piece but for UMAP. Pair them.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Decomposing signals in components (matrix factorization problems)
resources.annotation: The PCA reference plus the rest of the linear factor family in one place.

nodes.label: Train / validation / test splits
nodes.description: Why three splits, what cross-validation buys you, data leakage and how to spot it. The single most-violated rule in ML and the most common reason 'my model is great' fails in production.
nodes.doneWhen: You can identify data leakage in a sloppy ML pipeline review.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
resources.annotation: k-fold, stratified, time-series, leave-one-group-out. The full menu with the failure modes called out.

resources.title: Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance
resources.author: Kaufman et al.
resources.annotation: The classic taxonomy of leakage. Read once; you'll start spotting it in your own pipelines.

nodes.label: Bias-variance trade-off & regularization
nodes.description: Why models underfit, why they overfit, why regularization (L1, L2, dropout, early stopping) is the dial. The mental model behind every model-debugging conversation.
nodes.doneWhen: You can diagnose a learning curve as under- or overfitting and pick the right intervention.

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning — Chapter 2
resources.author: James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani
resources.annotation: Chapter 2 is the canonical treatment of bias-variance. Free PDF; ten pages that pay back a hundred times.

resources.title: Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off
resources.author: Belkin et al.
resources.annotation: The double-descent paper. Required when you wonder why a 175B model isn't overfitting; the modern picture is more interesting than the classical curve.

nodes.label: Evaluation metrics
nodes.description: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC for classification; MAE, MSE, R² for regression. When each one lies. The vocabulary of every results discussion.
nodes.doneWhen: You can pick the right metric for a problem and explain when accuracy is the wrong default.

resources.title: scikit-learn — Metrics and scoring
resources.annotation: The complete menu of metrics with the formulas and the gotchas inline. The page you'll bookmark.

resources.title: The Relationship Between Precision-Recall and ROC Curves
resources.author: Davis & Goadrich
resources.annotation: Why PR-AUC beats ROC-AUC on imbalanced data. A short read that prevents a common interview mistake.
